item.title: Shoonya: Zero-Socket In-Process Small Language Models for Graph Databases with Schema-Epoch KV Caching, Live Catalog Logit Masking, and Verifier-Advantage Distillation
item.description: arXiv:2611.28502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($\alpha \in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.
item.dc:creator: Madhulatha Mandarapu, Sandeep Kunkunuru

item.title: Bound to be Complete: Efficient Verification for SQL Equivalence via U-Expressions
item.description: arXiv:2611.28516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated verification of SQL query equivalence is a fundamental problem in database area. Recent works developed verifiers with guaranteed completeness, which can generate counterexamples to disprove non-equivalent queries and are useful in various scenarios. However, they have to solve complex formulas and can fail to produce counterexamples within a reasonable time budget. This paper presents a new complete verifier called SQLution, which not only greatly reduces the verification time, but also supports more SQL features. The key insight is to represent SQL semantics using U-expression, a functional algebra that can model SQL with significantly simpler formulas than prior works, thereby leading to more efficient SMT solving. To turn this insight into a practical verifier, SQLution further tackles two technical challenges associated with modeling SQL using U-expression, namely, the lack of tuple ordering and the presence of unbounded summations. In particular, to support tuple ordering, SQLution proposes order semantics encoding which combines U-expressions with first-order logic. To handle unbounded summation, SQLution introduces unbounded summation expansion to transform them into bounded summations, which can be directly encoded into FOL formulas. Evaluation shows that compared with state-of-the-art verifiers, SQLution can support all 271 non-equivalent query pairs derived from the Spider dataset and reduces verification time by up to 98.6%.
item.dc:creator: Haoran Ding, Zhaoguo Wang, Zuming Jiang, Haibo Chen, Jinyang Li, Ruzica Piskac

item.title: A Design Space for Data Agents: Insights from KDD Cup 2026
item.description: arXiv:2611.28970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data agents interpret analytical requests, gather evidence from heterogeneous sources, and compute results within finite resource budgets. We analyze the final code submissions of the ten highest-ranked teams in the KDD Cup 2026 Data Agents for Complex Data Analysis competition. We organize the observed design choices into three interacting layers, covering workflow orchestration, analytical functions, and working state. The comparison reveals recurring patterns for allocating computation in response to task progress, structuring evidence for computation and assessment, and preserving reusable artifacts with their provenance. Candidates that rely on the same evidence can inherit the same error, so interpreting their agreement requires tracing those dependencies. The design space motivates controlled evaluations of how resource allocation, evidence sharing, and targeted recovery affect task completion and correctness.
item.dc:creator: Boyan Li, Zhuowen Liang, Yupeng Xie, Xiaotian Lin, Xinyu Liu, Yizhang Zhu, Yuyu Luo

item.title: Mind the Trap As LLMs Guess the Data Model: Grain-Aware Guards Against Fan-out in Text-to-SQL and Its Benchmarks
item.description: arXiv:2611.29009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-SQL systems built on large language models (LLMs) often aggregate over one-to-many and many-to-many joins, a classic trap: when the joined rows repeat an entity, a SUM or COUNT counts it more than once, yet the query runs and returns a plausible number. We characterize these fan-out errors by one condition on the relation an aggregate reads, which depends on two facts a schema does not show: each measure's grain, and how many rows a join on each key repeats. An audit that tests the condition on the data finds distorted gold answers for 4.2% of the dev questions of BIRD, a widely used benchmark, and BIRD's later, independent revision changed 44% of the answers the audit flags as definite fan-out, against 16% of unflagged ones. We release BIRD-FanOut, 486 BIRD questions with reviewed gold, and GrainTraps, synthetic questions that set this trap and related ones. Across eight LLM agents, functional dependencies (FDs) computed from the data help no more than per-column statistics on GrainTraps, but grain-aware FDs, which also state each measure's grain and the repetition per key, cut fan-out errors on BIRD from 18.4% of runs to about 13%, also on held-out questions and without LLM judges. Accuracy rises less, because most remaining errors are not fan-out and BIRD's hints often prescribe the over-count. Text-to-SQL models should be given the grain of the data, and benchmark gold should be audited on the data. Code, data and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/ahmed-mahran/misqal
item.dc:creator: Ahmed M. Mahran

item.title: SJG: A Skyline Joint Graph for Multi-Component Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
item.description: arXiv:2611.29399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph-based indexes enable efficient approximate nearest neighbor search at scale by linking similar objects. In applications such as product retrieval and rental listing search, similarity depends on several components whose relative importance varies across queries. The challenge is that the index must select neighbors during construction, but the query weights that determine which objects are closest are not yet known. A straightforward approach is to index each component separately. However, merging the results of these searches can miss the nearest neighbor under the weighted distance. A joint graph allows a search to follow links across components, helping to avoid such misses, but selecting neighbors separately within each component can leave redundant edges, and keeping component hierarchies synchronized limits parallel construction. To address these limitations, we propose the Skyline Joint Graph (SJG). Although query weights can change the ranking of candidate neighbors, the dominance relation among them is independent of those weights. SJG exploits this property by pooling candidates across components and retaining the Skyline for each node, thereby enabling efficient approximate nearest neighbor search under different query weights while supporting parallel graph construction. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that SJG achieves up to $27.9\times$ the query throughput of baseline methods at 90% Recall@10, while accelerating single-threaded index construction by up to $201\times$. Its index requires at least 36% less space than the smallest baseline index.
item.dc:creator: Linyun Ma, Rui Mao

item.title: Look Before You Leap: Re-Architecting Disk-Resident Vector Search with TriVS
item.description: arXiv:2611.29948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Disk-resident approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) scales vector search beyond DRAM, yet state-of-the-art systems remain I/O-bound, even with fast SSDs and sophisticated I/O execution. To understand this bottleneck, we conduct an I/O-centric analysis that breaks each query down into an approach phase that locates a query-near region and a converge phase that resolves the final top-k. This analysis reveals complementary I/O tradeoffs: cluster-based search circumvents approach-phase I/O through in-memory routing but reads coarse-grained, full clusters during convergence, whereas graph-based search employs fine-grained, vector-level I/O throughout, enabling efficient convergence at the cost of inevitable I/O during the approach phase. To combine the complementary I/O benefits of the two granularities, we present TriVS, a new paradigm that re-architects disk-resident vector search as a trilogy: approach coarsely, distill progressively, and converge exactly. Its key innovations come in two parts. First, it decouples the approach and converge phases from a single search granularity, employing cluster-based search to avoid approach-phase I/O and leveraging vector-level I/O for efficient convergence. Second, to bridge the two granularities, it introduces a new in-memory distill phase between the original two, progressively reducing routed clusters to a vector-level shortlist using compact quantized vectors before disk access. Moreover, coarser clustering shrinks the centroid-routing index, allowing TriVS to reallocate existing memory to distillation rather than expand its memory budget. Our evaluation on five datasets spanning diverse vector types and scales shows that, at Recall@10=0.9, TriVS achieves on average 3.42X PipeANN's throughput, 51.2% lower latency, and 63.7% less disk I/O, while using less memory and storage than PipeANN.
item.dc:creator: Yizou Chen, Baotong Lu, Peiqi Yin, Zhisheng Hu, Qi Chen, Ming-Chang Yang

item.title: Toward a Scalable and Adaptive Evaluation Measure for Time Series Anomaly Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.30385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) is a fundamental task for time series analytics. Unlike other domains, where anomaly detection mainly focuses on point-based anomalies, TSAD must also handle range-based anomalies. Nevertheless, TSAD methods are commonly evaluated with measures inherited from classification, such as Precision and Recall, which require a threshold, or with threshold-independent ones, such as AUC, which ignore the temporal aspect of anomalies. To address these issues, the Volume Under the Surface (VUS) measure scores detectors across all thresholds and a range of buffer lengths and has been widely adopted. However, VUS has two limitations. First, VUS is computationally expensive, requiring 7 hours and 38 minutes to evaluate 32 detectors on the 870 TSB-AD time series. Second, VUS applies the same buffer lengths to every anomaly and detector, which can yield over-optimistic scores that hinder discrimination between accurate and mediocre detectors. We first introduce FastVUS, which computes VUS exactly and on average 76x faster by (i) computing all buffers in parallel, (ii) pruning irrelevant buffers for the existence reward, (iii) casting the confusion matrix as a single reduced matrix multiplication, (iv) computing VUS for every buffer length in one pass, and (v) discarding non-anomalous regions with a global mask. We also develop FastVUS-GPU, which recasts every step as batched tensor operations and reaches an average 304x speedup with a maximum error of $5\times10^{-3}$. Building on FastVUS, we introduce AutoVUS, an adaptive extension that compares each detection against a random baseline and selects the buffer length that maximizes the gain over it. Our case studies show that AutoVUS reduces over-optimistic scores and better separates accurate from mediocre detectors. We release FastVUS and AutoVUS as open source to promote time-aware evaluation at scale.
item.dc:creator: Emmanouil Sylligardos, Mingyi Huang, John Paparrizos, Pierre Senellart, Paul Boniol

item.title: SignalCount: Approximate Counts with Structured and Semantic Predicates in Seconds
item.description: arXiv:2611.30779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many applications store records with structured columns and a text document, and ask how many records in a filtered set meet a criterion that only a reader of the text can judge, such as "How many patients with type 2 diabetes, aged 40 to 70, stopped metformin because their blood sugar stayed high?" An interactive application needs this count in seconds, as the user types the criterion, to decide whether the matching set is worth materializing with a batch pipeline in which an LLM judges the records. Prior approximate query processing over such semantic predicates has an expensive model, the oracle, label a sample at query time, so every query waits for the oracle. We present SignalCount, a production system that answers COUNT queries with structured and semantic predicates and calls no oracle at query time, even for ad-hoc criteria. Its oracle is the production LLM judge, and the judge's logged verdicts calibrate, offline, the fast classifier that already runs in front of the judge. At query time, SignalCount counts the filtered set exactly and draws a uniform sample of at most 1,000 records in one columnar scan, scores the sample with the classifier, and multiplies the average calibrated probability by the exact count. Its 90% interval combines a sampling term with one-sided, rate-dependent margins for calibration error, fitted by split conformal prediction across tenants. In a multi-tenant production deployment, latency has a p99 of 3.8 s and stays flat as the filtered set grows beyond the sample. On tenants held out from fitting, the interval covers the count that the production pipeline returns in 92% of estimates, although estimates run about 15% high in aggregate, because a calibration nearly unbiased per record is still biased per criterion.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Agius-D'Arrigo, Zachary Zelner, Harrison Ju, Rushab Munot

item.title: SYCLDB: A Cross-Vendor Heterogeneous Analytical DBMS
item.description: arXiv:2611.30849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of AI and analytical workloads has increased the need for fast, interactive analytical data processing. This, in turn, has led to a surge of interest in designing accelerated analytical database engines that can exploit modern GPUs to scale computation. While GPUs provide the massive data-parallelism required by modern analytics, the software landscape remains dominated by closed-source, vendor-locked programming models, like CUDA, limiting portability across multi-vendor GPUs. In this work, we present SYCLDB, an end-to-end analytical database engine built upon the SYCL open standard, designed to enable efficient, hardware-agnostic execution across a wide range of accelerators using a single codebase. By implementing core relational operators as modular SYCL kernels, integrating them with a SQL frontend based on Apache Calcite and Apache Thrift, and supporting Apache Arrow for efficient columnar ingestion, SYCLDB reduces dependence on vendor-specific GPU programming stacks by enabling a single SYCL codebase to execute analytical query pipelines across Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA GPUs.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Advances in Databases and Information Systems (ADBIS 2026), LNCS 16937, pp. 31-47, Springer, Cham, 2027
item.dc:creator: Ivan Donchev Kabadzhov, Eugenio Marinelli, Raja Appuswamy

item.title: Zarc: Exact Nearest Neighbors over a Billion Vectors in Seconds
item.description: arXiv:2611.29252v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exact k-nearest-neighbor vector search lies on the critical path of machine learning systems, from sparse attention in the latest large language models (LLMs) to long-context memories and training-data deduplication. Exhaustive GPU search scans the whole dataset for every query, while approximate indexes return inexact neighbors. Recent methods skip almost every vector with a cheap half-precision proof that it lies too far away, but only on one GPU that holds the whole dataset. Our insight is to keep only the short rows of these proofs in GPU memory and to fetch the few remaining full vectors from host memory. Our system, Zarc, answers Euclidean, cosine, inner-product, and filtered queries exactly under updates. On four H100 GPUs, it answers 10,000 exact queries over one billion vectors in 1.1 seconds instead of five minutes. On eleven open LLMs, it retrieves the exact top-10 attention keys 2.2x to 13.1x faster than exhaustive search. In sparse attention over one million tokens, it runs 3.1x faster than bf16 selection with FlashInfer, which misses the exact top-64 for most queries.
item.dc:creator: Dongfang Zhao

item.title: Location-Aware Matching Statistics
item.description: arXiv:2611.30206v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Edit distance is the standard measure of string similarity, but its quadratic-time complexity is prohibitive for long strings. Popular linear-time alternatives, such as the $q$-gram distance, or the average common substring measure (ACS) that is based on matching statistics (MS), consider the substrings shared by the two input strings but not where they occur in each string. Yet in many real-world applications, e.g., when comparing document versions or co-recorded time series, a shared substring is really relevant only if its occurrences are close in position. We introduce Location-Aware Matching Statistics (LAMAS). Given strings $X$ and $Y$ and a displacement tolerance $d$, LAMAS reports, for every position $i$ of $Y$, the longest substring starting at $i$ that occurs in $X$ at a position $j$ with $|j-i|\le d$, together with the displacement $(j-i)$. MS is the special case of LAMAS with unbounded $d$. Our main result is an algorithm that solves LAMAS in $\mathcal{O}(n)$ time and space for strings of length at most $n$ and any $d$; this is optimal and matches the complexity of MS. The algorithm reduces LAMAS to predecessor and successor queries over a sliding window of suffix ranks and answers them in linear total time via a window decomposition and interval union-find. Experiments on 20 real datasets and synthetic data show that LAMAS substantially improves over MS and $q$-gram distance in similarity-based classification, top-$K$ retrieval, and clustering. It is competitive with edit distance and a constrained dynamic time warping variant in classification and generally outperforms a state-of-the-art method for top-$K$ retrieval under edit distance. Finally, our implementation of the main algorithm for LAMAS scales linearly in $n$ and does not slow down as $d$ grows.
item.dc:creator: Lorraine A. K. Ayad, Grigorios Loukides, Solon P. Pissis

item.title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
item.description: arXiv:2611.30483v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Kaya, Cevheri Bozoglan, Yusuf Gundogdu

item.title: SuSi-RAG: A Hybrid Graph RAG for Equipment Maintenance
item.description: arXiv:2611.30588v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the manufacturing domain, equipment maintenance tasks depend on expert knowledge. Their documentation is often stored in heterogeneous formats and sources. The enhancement of LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising for bridging the scattered knowledge, but traditional vector-based RAG shows weaknesses with two characteristics which are common in real maintenance queries: complex causal chains and cross-domain synthesis. To address this, we propose SuSi-RAG, a hybrid Graph RAG solution, that matches a user query and each maintenance record using subgraph similarity. This work shows an in-use system: SuSi-RAG has run on an active Bosch production line for more than eight months, handling 10,664 question-answer interactions and demonstrates upper bound answer accuracy of 96.25% (confirmed error rate 3.75%). In a proof-of-concept, SuSi-RAG improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from 61.5% to 96.2% and expert-rated answer quality from 44.9% to 84.1% against a vector-based baseline. We present an integrated operational feedback loop to update SuSi-RAG.
item.dc:creator: Hansi Zhang+, Wilma Johanna Schmidt+, Wanlin Yang, Xiaozhi Shen, Adrian Paschke, Evgeny Kharlamov

item.title: Trallie: from Free-Form Text to Structured Data with LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2611.30773v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Trallie is an open-source framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to perform information extraction (IE) from natural language sources with or without user guidance. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets or domain-specific training, Trallie enables the conversion of unstructured data into structured formats with minimal or no representative examples. The framework is designed with three key objectives: (i) reducing manual annotation by harnessing prompt-based zero-shot and few-shot capabilities of modern LLMs, (ii) flexibly parsing diverse document formats (i.e., HTML, PDF, TXT, and JSON), and (iii) improving accessibility for non-expert users by automatically inducing schemas from document collections, which can then be refined for extraction. We evaluate Trallie with open-weight LLMs on FDA 510(k) documents and on movie and university websites from SWDE. It outperforms previously reported systems when the target attributes are provided for text extraction and is competitive when it must discover attributes for the schema automatically. The project is available at https://github.com/PiSchool/trallie
item.dc:creator: Vijayasri Iyer, Cristiano De Nobili, Mubashir Hussain Shah, S\'ebastien Brati\`eres

item.title: Leveraging Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) for the Exchange of Wearable Inertial Sensor Data: Design and Development Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.30956v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Continuous monitoring with wearables can support the assessment of frailty, functional decline, and movement disorders, but raw inertial measurement unit (IMU) recordings are typically stored in proprietary files that electronic health records cannot exchange or interpret. HL7 Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standardizes health data exchange, yet existing FHIR profiles for personal health devices target spot measurements and short waveforms, not long multichannel motion recordings with their recording context and activity labels. We present WHIR (Wearable Health Interoperable Recordings), a FHIR R5-based information model and implementation guide for wearable IMU recordings. Metadata requirements were derived from a review of 23 published human activity recognition datasets and formalized in a FHIR-independent information model, which was then mapped to FHIR R5 and authored in FHIR Shorthand. Raw signals are kept in files referenced through DocumentReference resources, so that FHIR holds the metadata and activity labels. Terminology reuses SNOMED CT, LOINC, and ISO/IEEE 11073 concepts wherever available. The implementation guide defines 9 profiles, 4 extensions, 10 code systems, and 15 value sets; all artifacts and 67 example instances passed the conformance checks of the HL7 FHIR IG Publisher without errors. Two use cases, machine learning training data and automated home-based geriatric assessment, were implemented as conformant example instances, and we compare the model with the HL7 Personal Health Device Implementation Guide. WHIR provides a FHIR R5-conformant representation of wearable IMU recordings together with device metadata, sensor placement, and time-aligned activity labels, covering concepts that the Personal Health Device Implementation Guide does not address. The implementation guide and its sources are openly available for reuse and extension.
item.dc:creator: Gabriela Ciortuz, Joshua Wiedekopf, Hannes Ulrich, Hawzhin Hozhabr Pour, Sebastian Fudickar

item.title: MemForest: Write-Efficient Agent Memory with Decoupled Extraction and Hierarchical View Maintenance
item.description: arXiv:2605.23986v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-lived LLM agents maintain semantic views, such as fact records, profiles, and summaries, over a growing interaction history. Maintaining these views is a principal cost of agent memory: ingesting one conversation takes 15--53 minutes with leading memory systems, and most of this time lies on chains of dependent LLM calls that additional LLM capacity barely shortens. Because an LLM-generated view admits no delta rule, existing designs either serialize writes around revising views or give up fresh, reusable views. We present \textbf{MemForest}, which treats every view as a result derived from durable facts and recomputes it only from its children in a time-ordered tree. The dependency depth of view refresh then follows tree height rather than history length. Facts are extracted independently of existing memory, shared ancestors are refreshed once per batch, and independent views refresh in parallel. At query time, links from facts to trees recover details that compact views omit, and materialized interval views are reused for time-range aggregation. Against six released systems, MemForest builds memory \(4.7\times\) faster than EverMemOS on LongMemEval-S and \(8.8\times\) faster on LoCoMo. With Qwen3-30B, it matches EverMemOS on LoCoMo (84.1\%) and attains the highest LongMemEval-S accuracy (81.8\%).
item.dc:creator: Han Chen, Zining Zhang, Wenqi Pei, Bingsheng He, Ming Wu, Jason Zeng, Michael Heinrich, Wei Wu, Hongbao Zhang, Sen Gao

item.title: Revisiting Index Performance under High Cache-Miss Penalties
item.description: arXiv:2611.21835v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern data-intensive applications often query very large datasets, making index performance critical. Recent index structures exploit the fine-grained access capabilities of emerging storage devices such as DCPMM and CXL. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate indexes in isolation using saturated, closed-loop workloads that emphasize maximum throughput. Such workloads favor highly concurrent designs while overlooking the application work that follows an index lookup and competes for cache, memory bandwidth, and CPU resources. We present AuxBench - a microbenchmark that evaluates indexes as auxiliary access paths within larger application workloads. Using AuxBench, we evaluate four byte-addressable indexes under controlled post-lookup memory activity, concurrency, and request arrival patterns. Our experiments show that post-lookup memory activity can change the relative performance of competing indexes, that concurrency-oriented designs may lose their advantages when substantial application work is introduced, and that time-varying request arrivals can produce severe tail latency near saturation. These findings demonstrate why index-only benchmarks may not adequately predict performance in larger application workloads
item.dc:creator: Matthew M. Kim, Beomseok Nam

item.title: Relational Task Generation Language: A Declarative Specification Framework for Relational Deep Learning
item.description: arXiv:2609.01292v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Relational Deep Learning (RDL) has become a powerful paradigm for learning from multi-tabular data. However, manually defining RDL prediction tasks is a laborious process that frequently results in data leakage. To address this issue, we introduce the Relational Task Generation Language (RTGL), an open-source declarative language that streamlines RDL task formulation by abstracting away low-level SQL details. We showcase RTGL by reconstructing existing RDL benchmark tasks and uncovering their inconsistencies stemming from hand-written SQL definitions of RDL prediction targets, thereby underscoring the value of a dedicated declarative language. In addition, we demonstrate the practical utility of RTGL by designing various new tasks with diverse forms and target types. Our experiments confirm the robustness and usability of RTGL, as well as its integration with existing RDL frameworks, making it widely accessible to the community.
item.dc:creator: Oleksii Kolesnichenko, Jakub Pele\v{s}ka, Gustav \v{S}\'{\i}r

item.title: Containment of Conjunctive Queries with Negative Information over Semirings
item.description: arXiv:2610.27957v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the containment problem for (unions of) conjunctive queries ((U)CQs) with negative information on semiring-annotated databases. Our approach to negative information follows the treatment of negation proposed by Gr\"adel and Tannen (2017, 2019, 2021 and 2024) for first-order logic and fixed point logic which applies productively to large classes of semirings, including bounded distributive lattices, as well as the important provenance semirings studied for positive CQ containment by Green (2009). Negation features in (U)CQs along two dimensions: negated equalities (disequations), and negated relational atoms. We study complexity for each of them separately, as well as jointly. For disequations, we extend a methodology that proves the same complexity bounds as the ones already known for the standard Boolean semiring (in the second level of the polynomial hierarchy) for most semirings of interest. Two prominent exceptions are $\mathbb{N}[X]$ and Trio(X) where the complexity bound for containment is in the second level of the counting hierarchy. For CQs with negated relational atoms we show that the complexity, surprisingly, is the same as that of the containment of CQs without negation when one considers model-defining and provenance-tracking interpretations (namely, nondeterministic polynomial time). Interestingly, among bounded distributive lattices, the Boolean two-element case is the only one where the complexity of the problem continues to be hard for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy for model-defining interpretations. Furthermore, we show that the complexity increases again for distributive lattices if we focus on other classes of interpretations. Finally, we consider queries that have both negated equalities and negated relational atoms and show that the complexity of containment continues to be that of the case with just negated equalities.
item.dc:creator: Guillermo Badia, Carles Noguera, Gaia Petreni, Alice Portone, Val Tannen

item.title: High-Throughput Private Information Retrieval with on-CPU Accelerators
item.description: arXiv:2611.02376v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present AltoPIR, the first PIR system that exploits the capability of emerging on-CPU matrix accelerators such as Intel AMX. Unlike existing solutions, AltoPIR achieves high-performance PIR through efficient batching without requiring discrete accelerators. However, the on-CPU accelerator has only a few small registers and shares its core with request handling. As a result, it runs far below its peak rate while its operands arrive from memory, and it remains idle while its core handles requests. To keep the accelerator busy, we design mechanisms that reduce both the memory traffic of a batch and the core cycles spent on each request. Our experimental results show that AltoPIR outperforms existing CPU-based solutions by up to 50.1x.
item.dc:creator: Gyuyeong Kim
